newsitem.title: CANADA: Japan, Peru begin formal summit on hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Japan, Peru begin formal summit on hostage crisis.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori began a hastily arranged summit in Toronto on Saturday, seeking to resolve differences over the prolonged Lima hostage crisis.

The two leaders shook hands and exchanged pleasantries in view of photographers before their private talks began at a downtown Toronto hotel. Each side was accompanied by a few aides and a translator.

"Although I was tired because of my trip, I could not sleep well because I was thinking about various things ... about the summit," Hashimoto told reporters on Saturday before the meeting, which was expected to last about two hours.
"I become tense when I think of my obligation to let a bright light be cast on the result of the summit, paving the way for a solution to the hostage crisis," he said.
On Friday, the two leaders met briefly and informally.

Saturday's summit takes place in a climate of rising tension in the standoff between Peruvian police and guerrillas who have been holding 72 diplomats and businessmen captive in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima since Dec. 17.

"What we are worried about is that communications between the Peruvian government and the rebels have broken down and tensions have been running high," a Japanese government official said late on Friday.

Peru's negotiations with about 15 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas occupying the residence have halted over Fujimori's refusal to consider the key rebel demand that 400 of their comrades be released from Peruvian jails.

Hashimoto told reporters on the plane to Toronto he would "frankly ask" Fujimori to open negotiations with the MRTA. He was expected to try to convince the Peruvian leader to place the release of the rebel's jailed comrades on the agenda for peace talks, a Japanese government source said.

Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, has a hawkish reputation against guerrilla movements, built mainly on his record of crushing the Marxist Shining Path rebel movement. He has vowed to wipe out "terrorism" in Peru.
Although his younger brother Pedro is among the group of diplomats, cabinet ministers, generals and security chiefs held captive by the rebels, he has sworn not to cave into their demands.

"We are not going to give in to the terrorists's demands," Fujimori said in an interview with an Argentine newspaper before leaving for Canada. "As time goes by, offers made by the government are being progressively reduced."
Japan's concern that the standoff could end in bloodshed deepened this week after a series of provocative actions by Peruvian police outside the ambassador's compound.

Peruvian authorities said the police actions -- which included rumbling past the compound in armoured vehicles and blasting music at the residence at odd hours -- were aimed at wearing down the resistance of the rebels.
The Japanese and Peruvian leaders were due to hold a joint news conference after the meeting. They will afterward attend a lunch hosted by Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien.
